body: Both men won through enormous volumes of primary research applied to small, under-followed opportunities while their capital was small. Scale shrank both of their edges. The most-repeated anecdotes (cigar-butt brilliance, "buy what you know," "Magellan investors lost money") get their causes wrong. Buffett's lifetime results come largely from cheap, durable leverage and decades of survival. Lynch's come from relentless legwork during a favorable 13-year window.

`event:india-sme-ipo-mania-2024` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: india, blowup, ipo, smallcap, redflag, policy, governance

SME IPOs boomed in FY24 and FY25: the RBI noted a strong surge driven by retail participation, and the BSE SME IPO index outperformed the mainboard IPO index and the Sensex. Symbol of the mania (from memory, not re-verified here): Resourceful Automobile (Aug 2024), a Delhi two-wheeler dealer with two showrooms and a handful of employees, raised ~Rs 12 crore and was oversubscribed ~400x; many SME issues were subscribed hundreds of times. SEBI officials warned in 2024 of manipulation, inflated financials and 'pump and dump' in SME listings; NSE capped SME listing-day gains at 90% (2024, from memory). SEBI board on 18 Dec 2024 tightened norms (in ICDR by Mar 2025): minimum EBITDA of Rs 1 crore in 2 of 3 years, minimum application of two lots, and other limits; exchanges applied new SME rules from 1 July 2025; by May 2025 some SME IPOs excluded retail bids under Rs 2 lakh. In Oct 2026 a SEBI working group/consultation proposed a further overhaul (e.g., scrapping compulsory 3-year market making). Post-listing, many 2024 SME stocks fell sharply in 2025 (no index-level figure found; unverified). Signals at the top: absurd subscription multiples for tiny, unknown issuers, listing pops used as the investment case, promoter-linked merchant bankers, regulator warnings. Lesson: same as the 1990s IPO boom - when the quality of what is being listed collapses, expect the worst losses there first.
